claim: Chimeric RNAs have been found in both cancerous and healthy human cells.
source: Chimeric RNAs have been found in both cancerous and healthy human cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Chimeric RNAs have regulatory effects on human stem/progenitor cell differentiation, stemness maintenance, and central nervous system development.
source: They have regulatory effects on human stem/progenitor cell differentiation, stemness maintenance, and central nervous system development.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge from prior research in the field.

claim: The presence of chimeric RNAs in human retinal cells and their physiological functions in retinal development were previously unknown.
source: However, whether they are present in human retinal cells and their physiological functions in the retinal development remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The study presents an expression atlas of chimeric RNAs throughout developing retinal organoids from days 0 to 120.
source: Based on the human embryonic stem cell-derived retinal organoids (ROs) spanning from days 0 to 120, we present the expression atlas of chimeric RNAs throughout the developing ROs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA sequencing data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study confirmed the existence of some common chimeric RNAs during retinal development.
source: We confirmed the existence of some common chimeric RNAs and also discovered many novel chimeric RNAs during retinal development.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA sequencing data and validation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The study discovered many novel chimeric RNAs during retinal development.
source: We confirmed the existence of some common chimeric RNAs and also discovered many novel chimeric RNAs during retinal development.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Downregulation of CTNNBIP1-CLSTN1 (CTCL) caused precocious neuronal differentiation and a marked reduction of neural progenitors in human cerebral organoids.
source: We focused on CTNNBIP1-CLSTN1 (CTCL) whose downregulation caused precocious neuronal differentiation and a marked reduction of neural progenitors in human cerebral organoids.
evidence: This statement references findings from a previous study (Ou et al., 2021) as cited in the introduction.

claim: CTCL is universally present in human retinas, retinal organoids, and retinal cell lines.
source: CTCL is universally present in human retinas, ROs, and retinal cell lines, and its loss-of-function biases the progenitor cells toward retinal pigment epithelial cell fate at the expense of retinal cells.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR validation and Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Loss-of-function of CTCL biases progenitor cells toward retinal pigment epithelial cell fate at the expense of retinal cells.
source: CTCL is universally present in human retinas, ROs, and retinal cell lines, and its loss-of-function biases the progenitor cells toward retinal pigment epithelial cell fate at the expense of retinal cells.
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiments and immunostaining data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The human retina is a laminar structure with a large number of different component cells that form morphologically and functionally distinct circuits.
source: The human retina is a laminar structure with a large number of different component cells that form morphologically and functionally distinct circuits. They work in parallel and in combination to produce complex visual output (Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hoon et al., 2014.

claim: During retinogenesis, different subtypes of neurons are generated from the same group of retinal progenitor cells and precisely self-assemble into a functionally mature retina.
source: During retinogenesis, different subtypes of neurons are generated from the same group of retinal progenitor cells (RPCs) and precisely self-assemble into a functionally mature retina (Masland, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Masland, 2012.

claim: Lu et al. identified an unexpected role for ATOH7 expression in the regulation of photoreceptor specification during late retinogenesis.
source: Lu et al. identified an unexpected role for ATOH7 expression in the regulation of photoreceptor specification during late retinogenesis as well as the enriched bivalent modification of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 in human but not in murine retinogenesis (Lu et al., 2020), further underscoring the limitations of using mouse models to study the human retina and transcriptional regulation in human retinogenesis.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: Bivalent modification of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 is enriched in human but not in murine retinogenesis.
source: Lu et al. identified an unexpected role for ATOH7 expression in the regulation of photoreceptor specification during late retinogenesis as well as the enriched bivalent modification of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 in human but not in murine retinogenesis (Lu et al., 2020), further underscoring the limitations of using mouse models to study the human retina and transcriptional regulation in human retinogenesis.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: Retinal organoids have high similarity to human retina in terms of molecular features, cell types, and developmental rates.
source: Many groups have used ROs to conduct studies related to human retinal development and have solved a basket of previously unsolvable problems, confirming the high similarity between ROs and human retina in terms of molecular features, cell types, and developmental rates (Cowan et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cowan et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020.

claim: Retinoblastoma tumor cells are derived from cone precursor cells.
source: For example, together with other groups, we have used ROs to confirm that retinoblastoma tumor cells are derived from cone precursor cells (Clevers, 2016; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Clevers, 2016; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Chimeric RNAs are the ligation products of two or even more DNA or RNA sequences before or after transcription.
source: Chimeric RNAs are the ligation products of two or even more DNA or RNA sequences before or after transcription.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chimeric RNAs can be further translated into proteins in addition to their RNA form.
source: They can be further translated into proteins in addition to their RNA form, increasing the richness of the transcriptome and proteome.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about chimeric RNAs.

claim: Chimeric RNAs are widely present in human normal and tumor tissues as part of the transcriptome and can regulate the activities of individual cells.
source: Previous studies of chimeric RNAs have focused on tumors and larger tissues and organs, and found that chimeric RNAs are widely present in human normal and tumor tissues as part of the transcriptome and can regulate the activities of individual cells (Elfman and Li, 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Mertens et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Elfman and Li, 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Mertens et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2020.

claim: Chimeric RNAs in normal human cortex increase with age and show differences in individual cells and tissues.
source: It has been shown that chimeric RNAs in normal human cortex increase with age and show differences in individual cells and tissues (Mehani et al., 2020), highlighting the critical role of chimeric RNAs in central nervous system (CNS) development and cell lineage maintenance.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mehani et al., 2020.

claim: Downregulation of CTNNBIP1-CLSTN1 (CTCL) affects the growth of cerebral organoids, causing premature neuronal differentiation, and a marked reduction of neural progenitors.
source: In 2021, Luo's group found that downregulation of CTNNBIP1-CLSTN1 (CTCL) affects the growth of cerebral organoids, causing premature neuronal differentiation, and a marked reduction of neural progenitors (Ou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ou et al., 2021.

claim: Chimeric RNAs were continuously expressed during retinal organoid development.
source: Chimeric RNAs were continuously expressed during RO development (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the circos plots shown in Figure 2A displaying chimeric RNAs at all developmental stages.

claim: The number of intra-chromosomal chimeric RNAs increased with the development of retinal organoids.
source: While the number of intra-chromosomal chimeric RNAs increased with the development of ROs (r2 = 0.93, p = 0.00076, Pearson's correlation analysis), there was no such trend for inter-chromosomal chimeric RNAs (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson's correlation analysis (r2 = 0.93, p = 0.00076) and data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: There was no trend of increase for inter-chromosomal chimeric RNAs during retinal organoid development.
source: While the number of intra-chromosomal chimeric RNAs increased with the development of ROs (r2 = 0.93, p = 0.00076, Pearson's correlation analysis), there was no such trend for inter-chromosomal chimeric RNAs (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: In-frame chimeric RNAs represent 11.2% of the top three categories of chimeric events.
source: In the top three categories, the number of 'In-frame' chimeric RNAs was 11.2%, followed by 'CDS(truncated)_UTR' (10.7%) and 'UTR_UTR' (10.7%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of chimeric RNAs were formed between two protein-coding genes (61.9%).
source: The majority of chimeric RNAs were formed between two protein-coding genes (61.9%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the biotype quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The canonical AG/GT donor–acceptor motif had the highest position weight at the fusion site of parental genes.
source: Next, we examined the motifs covering 10 bp sequences immediately upstream or downstream of the fusion site of parental genes and found that the canonical AG/GT donor–acceptor motif had the highest position weight (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the motif analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of chimeric RNAs did not correlate with the expression of the parental genes.
source: In addition, we also found that the expression of the chimeric RNAs did not correlate with the expression of the parental genes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D (p > 0.05).

claim: Four isoforms of CTCL, joined by alternative splicing of the parent pre-mRNAs, were detected in the retinal organoids by RNA-seq.
source: CTCL has been shown to have a regulatory role in human cerebral development. Similarly, four isoforms of CTCL, joined by alternative splicing of the parent pre-mRNAs, were detected in the ROs by RNA-seq.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: In-frame CTCL was dynamically expressed during retinal organoid development with two obvious higher expression timepoints at D60 and D120.
source: In-frame CTCL can be further translated into chimeric proteins, and we think that it plays a more critical role than the other three isoforms. It was dynamically expressed during RO development and there were two obvious higher expression timepoints at D60 and D120 (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the expression data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: At D60, the In-frame, UTR_CDS(truncated)-1, and CDS(truncated)Intronic CTCL isoforms were confirmed but UTR_CDS(truncated)-2 CTCL was not detected.
source: At D60, the In-frame, UTR_CDS(truncated)-1, and CDS(truncated)Intronic CTCL isoforms were confirmed but UTR_CDS(truncated)-2 CTCL was not detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR and Sanger sequencing validation shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The In-frame CTCL was consistently identified in human retinas, iPSCs1/iPSCs2/iPSCs3-derived ROs, and H9 cells, but not in mouse retinas.
source: Indeed, the In-frame CTCL was consistently identified in human retinas, iPSCs1/iPSCs2/iPSCs3-derived ROs, and H9 cells, but not in the mouse retinas (Figure 5—source data 1; Figure 5—source data 2; Figure 5—source data 3; Figure 5—source data 4; Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR and Sanger sequencing validation shown in Figure 5.

claim: All nine human retinal samples from the GEO database yielded uniformly positive results for CTCL.
source: Moreover, we also screened CTCL using the retinal transcriptome sequencing data available in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, all of the nine human retinal samples yielded uniformly positive results (Table 1; Sun et al., 2019; Zauhar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Table 1 and citations to Sun et al., 2019; Zauhar et al., 2022.

claim: CTCL is universally generated in human retinas in vivo, retinal organoids, and retinal cell lines in vitro, but not a phenomenon of the H9 cell line exclusively.
source: These results suggest that CTCL is universally generated in human retinas in vivo, ROs, and retinal cell lines in vitro, but not a phenomenon of the H9 cell line exclusively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation data from multiple cell lines and samples shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Compared with the scramble shRNA group, the In-frame CTCL RNA level was reduced to approximately 70% in the shCTCL group.
source: Compared with the scramble shRNA group, the In-frame CTCL RNA level was reduced to approximately 70% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the knockdown efficiency data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The RNA levels of the parental genes, CTNNBIP1 and CLSTN1, showed no significant differences compared to the scramble shRNA group.
source: The RNA levels of the parental genes, CTNNBIP1 and CLSTN1, showed no significant differences compared to the scramble shRNA group (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ShCTCL-transfected organoids showed thinner outer layers with much less CRX expression compared to scramble shRNA-transfected organoids.
source: D60 scramble shRNA-transfected retinal organoids (ROs) displayed a typical morphology of ROs with the expression of CRX. ShCTCL-transfected organoids showed thinner outer layers with much less CRX expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the live-cell imaging and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is a dramatic decrease in the outer layer thickness in the shCTCL group compared to the scramble shRNA group.
source: The average thickness of the outer layers in those two groups was calculated (Figure 6D, outer layer indicated with orange arrows, live-cell imaging), and there is a dramatic decrease in the outer layer thickness in the shCTCL group.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 6D (t-test, ****, p < 0.0001).

claim: PAX6 was highly expressed in CTCL-knockdown organoids, but OTX2 was much less expressed.
source: To identify the aberrations in cell fate specification caused by CTCL knockdown, we examined the organoids with RPC-specific markers, PAX6 and OTX2. It was shown that PAX6 was highly expressed, but OTX2 was much less, and CRX appeared where GFP (shCTCL) was relatively lower (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunostaining data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CRX is highly expressed in photoreceptors and precursors but low in mature RPE.
source: CRX is known to be highly expressed in photoreceptors and precursors but low in mature RPE (Lidgerwood et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lidgerwood et al., 2021.

claim: CTCL knockdown would promote the RPE cell fate at the expense of neural retinal cells.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that CTCL is essential for the ROs' differentiation and that CTCL knockdown would promote the RPE cell fate at the expense of neural retinal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining data showing RPE markers in shCTCL organoids (Figure 6E-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).

claim: 3901 differentially expressed genes were obtained between shCTCL- and scramble shRNA-treated organoids, with 2720 upregulated and 1181 downregulated.
source: We obtained 3901 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (shCTCL vs. scramble shRNA, |Log2(fold change)| > 1, p-value <0.05), among which 2720 were upregulated and 1181 downregulated (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Upregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways associated with extracellular matrix organization, morphogenesis, and epithelial cell differentiation.
source: Upregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways associated with extracellular matrix organization, morphogenesis, and epithelial cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Downregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in neurogenesis-associated pathways.
source: On the other hand, downregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in the neurogenesis-associated pathways (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Genes of RPE, ocular corneal, and conjunctival epithelial cells were significantly upregulated in shCTCL organoids.
source: GSEA analysis with c8 as the reference gene set (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005) revealed that genes of RPE, ocular corneal, and conjunctival epithelial cells were significantly upregulated in shCTCL organoids; however, all genes related to neural retinal component cells (photoreceptor cells, Müller glial cells, horizontal cell, amacrine cell, and retinal ganglion cell) were downregulated (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7D, with citations to Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005.

claim: All genes related to neural retinal component cells (photoreceptor cells, Müller glial cells, horizontal cell, amacrine cell, and retinal ganglion cell) were downregulated in shCTCL organoids.
source: GSEA analysis with c8 as the reference gene set (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005) revealed that genes of RPE, ocular corneal, and conjunctival epithelial cells were significantly upregulated in shCTCL organoids; however, all genes related to neural retinal component cells (photoreceptor cells, Müller glial cells, horizontal cell, amacrine cell, and retinal ganglion cell) were downregulated (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7D, with citations to Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005.

claim: The expression pattern of RPE-related genes in shCTCL organoids was closer to that of RPE from induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Moreover, the expression pattern of RPE-related genes in shCTCL organoids was closer to that of RPE from induced pluripotent stem cells (Maruotti et al., 2015; Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, with a citation to Maruotti et al., 2015.

claim: CTCL remains in a low expression state during RPE development.
source: At the same time, CTCL remains in a low expression state during RPE development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The most significantly enriched pathway in shCTCL organoids was epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: To further explore the molecular mechanisms involved in this process, we performed the GSEA analysis using hallmark gene sets (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005). The most significantly enriched pathway was epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7F, with citations to Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005.

claim: Most of the EMT-related genes were relatively highly expressed in shCTCL-treated organoids.
source: And most of the EMT-related genes were relatively highly expressed in shCTCL-treated organoids (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) (Figure 7G), which is particularly essential for neural crest delamination in vertebrates and the generation of different tissues during development (Kim et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2, with a citation to Kim et al., 2014b.

claim: EMT is particularly essential for neural crest delamination in vertebrates and the generation of different tissues during development.
source: And most of the EMT-related genes were relatively highly expressed in shCTCL-treated organoids (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) (Figure 7G), which is particularly essential for neural crest delamination in vertebrates and the generation of different tissues during development (Kim et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014b.

claim: The downregulation of CTCL expression activated the EMT pathway which altered the directions of cell differentiation.
source: Therefore, the downregulation of CTCL expression activated the EMT pathway which altered the directions of cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA analysis and gene expression data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: The first chimeric RNA that lacks DNA alterations is AML1-ETO, which is associated with acute myeloid leukemia.
source: The first chimeric RNA that lacks DNA alterations is AML1-ETO, which is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (Langabeer et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Langabeer et al., 1997.

claim: Cis-splicing between neighboring genes was found to generate chimeric RNAs, such as the CTCF-sensitive cis-spliced fusion RNAs ADCK4-NUMBL in prostate cancer.
source: Subsequently, cis-splicing between neighboring genes was also found to generate chimeric RNAs, such as the CTCF-sensitive cis-spliced fusion RNAs ADCK4-NUMBL in prostate cancer (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2015.

claim: Chimeric RNAs can be generated by long-range inter- and intra-chromosomal trans-splicing.
source: In addition, chimeric RNAs can be generated by long-range inter- and intra-chromosomal trans-splicing (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: PAX3-FOXO1 was initially identified as a biomarker for alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma but was later found to be present during normal muscle differentiation.
source: For example, PAX3-FOXO1 was initially identified as a biomarker for alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (Singh et al., 2022), but was later found to be present during normal muscle differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2022.

claim: PAX3-FOXO1 is transiently required for muscle lineage commitment.
source: PAX3-FOXO1 is transiently required for muscle lineage commitment (Xie et al., 2019), and can escape miR-495 regulation during muscle differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xie et al., 2019.

claim: If PAX3-FOXO1 is not withdrawn at the right timing, it can lead to tumorigenesis.
source: If PAX3-FOXO1 is not withdrawn at the right timing, it can lead to tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of PAX3-FOXO1's role in normal development versus cancer.

claim: DUS4L-BCAP29 was originally identified in gastric cancer, where it promotes cell proliferation.
source: DUS4L-BCAP29 was originally identified in gastric cancer, where it promotes cell proliferation and is therefore considered to have tumorigenic potential (Kim et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2014a.

claim: DUS4L-BCAP29 was subsequently identified in human non-cancerous tissues.
source: DUS4L-BCAP29 was subsequently identified in human non-cancerous tissues (Tang et al., 2017), and its role in promoting cell proliferation is not unique to cancer cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: DUS4L-BCAP29 is a chimeric RNA present in normal physiology with a function in promoting neural differentiation.
source: It is a chimeric RNA present in normal physiology with a function in promoting neural differentiation (Tang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2019.

claim: In-frame CTCL is generated by cis-splicing fusion of the first 5 exons of CTNNBIP1 and the last 17 exons of CLSTN1.
source: In-frame CTCL is generated by cis-splicing fusion of the first 5 exons of CTNNBIP1 and the last 17 exons of CLSTN1.
evidence: This is a structural description based on the RNA-seq and sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 5′ parental gene CTNNBIP1 encodes a receptor for β-catenin, and their binding promotes the catabolism of β-catenin, which in turn puts the Wnt pathway in an inactive state.
source: The 5′ parental gene CTNNBIP1 encodes a receptor for β-catenin, and their binding promotes the catabolism of β-catenin, which in turn puts the Wnt pathway in an inactive state (Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2018.

claim: CTNNBIP1 mutation has been shown to be associated with anterior segment dysgenesis 5 in the human disease database MalaCards.
source: Its mutation has been shown to be associated with anterior segment dysgenesis 5 in the human disease database MalaCards (https://www.malacards.org/).
evidence: This statement references information from the MalaCards database.

claim: CLSTN1 is a member of the calsyntenin family, a subset of the cadherin superfamily.
source: CLSTN1 is a member of the calsyntenin family, a subset of the cadherin superfamily.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CLSTN1.

claim: CLSTN1 can mediate the axonal anterograde transport of certain types of vesicles.
source: It can mediate the axonal anterograde transport of certain types of vesicles (Nagase et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nagase et al., 1998.

claim: CTCL could fine-tune Wnt signaling to regulate cerebral development.
source: Previous report demonstrated that CTCL could fine-tune Wnt signaling to regulate cerebral development (Ou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ou et al., 2021.

claim: The GSEA and DEG functional enrichment results did not show significant changes in Wnt signaling pathway or vesicular trafficking pathways in CTCL-knockdown organoids.
source: However, surprisingly, the GSEA and DEG functional enrichment results did not show significant changes in these two biological pathways (Figure 6C, D, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GSEA and functional enrichment analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The same chimeric RNAs may function differently in close tissues.
source: The differences between the shCTCL- or scramble shRNA-treated organoids were mainly in EMT, extracellular matrix organization, morphogenesis, epithelial cell differentiation, and neurogenesis-associated pathways, suggesting that even the same chimeric RNAs may function differently in close tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of CTCL function in cerebral versus retinal organoids.

claim: This study revealed for the first time a key role of chimeric RNAs in human retinal development.
source: This study revealed for the first time a key role of chimeric RNAs in human retinal development, providing new insights into the role of chimeric RNAs in regulating tissue development.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: At D30 of differentiation, the retinal organoid outermost layer with translucent neural retina structures was visible.
source: At D30 of differentiation, the RO outermost layer with translucent NR structures was visible.
evidence: This is a description of the organoid morphology observed during the differentiation process.

claim: At D105 of differentiation, retinal organoids could be seen with the formation of RPE.
source: At D105 of differentiation, ROs could be seen with the formation of RPE.
evidence: This is a description of the organoid morphology observed during the differentiation process.

claim: At D120 of differentiation, the outer segments of photoreceptor cells were seen on the surface of retinal organoids.
source: At D120 of differentiation, the outer segments of photoreceptor cells were seen on the surface of ROs.
evidence: This is a description of the organoid morphology observed during the differentiation process.

claim: Retinal organoids covering eight developmental stages from D0, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, and 105–120 correspond to in vivo developmental stages D0, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, and 120.
source: Using FusionCatcher software, we examined chimeric RNAs in human ROs covering eight developmental stages from D0, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, and 105–120, corresponding to in vivo developmental stages D0, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, and 120 (Cowan et al., 2020), respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cowan et al., 2020.

claim: Each developmental stage included two to three biological replicates with a total of N = 22 samples.
source: Each stage included two to three biological replicates (a total of N = 22), and each replicate contained approximately 100 ROs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the RNA sequencing study.

claim: Each replicate contained approximately 100 retinal organoids.
source: Each stage included two to three biological replicates (a total of N = 22), and each replicate contained approximately 100 ROs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the RNA sequencing study.

claim: Splicing events were considered as positive chimeric RNA candidates only if spanning unique reads were detected at least once.
source: To reduce false positives, splicing events were considered as positive chimeric RNA candidates only if spanning unique reads were detected at least once (Figure 1, bottom panel).
evidence: This describes the criteria used for identifying chimeric RNAs in the study.

claim: CTCL has a positive role in the normal development of retinal organoids.
source: These results suggest that CTCL has a positive role in the normal development of ROs and that CTCL deficiency would promote the differentiation of RPCs toward RPE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown experiments and their effects on organoid development.

claim: CTCL deficiency would promote the differentiation of RPCs toward RPE.
source: These results suggest that CTCL has a positive role in the normal development of ROs and that CTCL deficiency would promote the differentiation of RPCs toward RPE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown experiments showing increased RPE markers.

claim: RPCs with a relatively high level of CTCL expression will differentiate into neural retina.
source: RPCs with a relatively high level of CTCL expression will differentiate into NR, while those with a relatively low level of CTCL will differentiate toward RPE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown experiments and expression patterns observed.

claim: RPCs with a relatively low level of CTCL will differentiate toward RPE.
source: RPCs with a relatively high level of CTCL expression will differentiate into NR, while those with a relatively low level of CTCL will differentiate toward RPE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown experiments and expression patterns observed.
